name: Bayeux Tapestry
summary: An eleventh-century embroidered narrative of the Norman Conquest, preserved at Bayeux.
details: An eleventh-century embroidered narrative of the Norman Conquest, preserved at Bayeux.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Bayeux Tapestry is an eleventh-century embroidery on linen that narrates the events leading to the Norman Conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings. It is roughly 70 meters long and combines Latin captions with scenes of oath-taking, shipbuilding, feasting, battle, death, and royal display.

Its power comes from the way it works as both evidence and argument. It preserves visual information about ships, weapons, horses, clothing, architecture, and ceremony, while also presenting a Norman-friendly account in which Harold Godwinson's oath and William's victory support the legitimacy of conquest.

contentSections.title: Description
paragraphs: Despite its name, the object is not a woven tapestry but an embroidery, worked mainly in wool thread on linen. Its long frieze format creates a moving narrative: figures gesture, ride, feast, build ships, cross the Channel, and fight across a continuous visual field.

The upper and lower borders contain animals, fables, decorative motifs, and occasional scenes that comment on or complicate the central story. The Latin tituli identify figures and actions, but much of the interpretation depends on visual sequencing and political context.

contentSections.title: Origin and dating
paragraphs: The tapestry was probably made in the late eleventh century, close enough to the conquest to preserve early Norman memory of 1066. Its exact patron remains debated, though Odo of Bayeux, William the Conqueror's half-brother, is often discussed because Bayeux and several of Odo's followers appear prominently.

The workshop is also uncertain. Some scholars have argued for English embroidery traditions because Anglo-Saxon needlework was highly regarded, while the narrative serves Norman political interests. The object therefore sits at the intersection of conquest, patronage, and cross-Channel artistic skill.

contentSections.title: Historical context
paragraphs: The narrative begins with Edward the Confessor and follows Harold's journey to Normandy, his oath to William, the appearance of Halley's Comet, the Norman invasion fleet, and the battle itself. It frames Hastings as the resolution of a broken oath and a contested succession.

Historians use it cautiously. The tapestry is invaluable for material culture and Norman memory, but it is not neutral reportage. It omits, compresses, and emphasizes events to make conquest appear legitimate and providential.

contentSections.title: Current location and legacy
paragraphs: The tapestry is preserved at Bayeux in Normandy, where its survival is extraordinary given its age, textile fragility, and political importance. It has become one of the most recognizable medieval objects in the world.

Its legacy reaches beyond art history. The Bayeux Tapestry shapes how modern readers imagine 1066: the ships, the cavalry, the shield wall, the death of Harold, and the visual drama of conquest all owe much to this single embroidered narrative.
